title: Orange Juice for a Hangover: Does It Help or Hurt Your Stomach?
excerpt: Is orange juice good for a hangover? What vitamin C, sugar, and potassium can and can't do, why the acidity can backfire on a sore stomach, and what to drink instead.
metaDescription: Does orange juice help a hangover? What its vitamin C, sugar, and potassium can and can't do, when its acidity makes things worse, and better options.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** orange juice can help a hangover a little, but not for the reason most people think. It's a quick way to get fluid, easy sugar, and potassium into a body that is mildly dehydrated and may be running low on energy. The vitamin C is the part everyone talks about, and it's the part with the weakest evidence. There is no good evidence that orange juice, or vitamin C on its own, shortens a hangover in a meaningful way. And because orange juice is acidic, it can make heartburn or a sore stomach worse the morning after.

**The quick rules:** If your stomach feels fine, a small glass of orange juice alongside water and some food is a perfectly reasonable part of a hangover morning. If you have heartburn, a burning stomach, or you've been throwing up, start with water or an electrolyte drink and something bland, and save the juice for later. Dilute it if it stings. Don't add vodka or champagne to it. And don't count on it to fix anything the time and rest won't.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is miserable but passes within a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe stomach pain, you're confused or very hard to wake, you have a seizure, or your symptoms keep getting worse instead of better. If someone is passed out and can't be woken, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin, call 911: those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and juice or coffee won't help. If you have diabetes, check your blood sugar, because alcohol can push it dangerously low.

## Why People Reach for Orange Juice After Drinking

Orange juice has a reputation as a hangover drink for a few understandable reasons. It's in nearly every fridge. It's cold and sweet, which feels good when you're queasy and tired. It's associated with breakfast and with being healthy. And the idea that vitamin C "flushes out" alcohol or toxins has been repeated for decades.

Some of that intuition is reasonable, and some of it isn't. To sort it out, it helps to know what actually causes a hangover. Researchers still don't fully agree, but the main contributors seem to be:

- **Mild dehydration.** Alcohol makes your kidneys release more water than usual by suppressing a hormone that normally holds fluid in.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, and the levels of inflammatory signaling molecules have been linked to how bad people feel.
- **Acetaldehyde.** This is the toxic compound your liver makes when it starts breaking down alcohol, before it converts it into something harmless.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments sleep later in the night.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol increases stomach acid and irritates the stomach lining.
- **Low blood sugar in some people.** Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to release glucose into the blood, which can leave you shaky, weak, and foggy.

Orange juice touches a few of these (fluid, blood sugar, possibly a small antioxidant effect) and does nothing for others (sleep, acetaldehyde). On one of them, stomach irritation, it can actually make things worse.

## What's Actually in a Glass of Orange Juice

Here's roughly what you get in one cup (8 fluid ounces, about 240 ml) of 100% orange juice. Exact numbers vary by brand and whether it's fresh, from concentrate, or fortified, so treat these as ballpark figures.

| Nutrient | Approximate amount per cup | Why it matters after drinking |
|---|---|---|
| Water | Mostly water (around 88%) | Helps replace fluid lost overnight |
| Natural sugar | About 20 to 25 g | Quick energy, can help if blood sugar is low |
| Calories | About 110 | Easy fuel when solid food feels impossible |
| Vitamin C | Roughly 80 to 125 mg | More than a full day's recommended amount for most adults |
| Potassium | About 450 to 500 mg | An electrolyte you lose through urine |
| Sodium | Very little (a few mg) | The electrolyte you lose most when you sweat or vomit |
| Folate | A useful amount | A B vitamin that heavy drinking can deplete over time |
| Acidity | pH around 3.3 to 4 | Can sting an already irritated stomach or esophagus |

Two things stand out. First, one glass already gives you more vitamin C than you need in a day, so the idea of "loading up" on it doesn't hold much water. Second, orange juice is rich in potassium but has almost no sodium, which matters for rehydration (more on that below).

## Vitamin C and Hangovers: What the Evidence Says

This is the heart of the orange juice question, so it's worth being specific.

**The theory.** Alcohol metabolism creates oxidative stress, which is a kind of chemical wear and tear on cells. Vitamin C is an antioxidant. Heavy drinkers often have lower vitamin C levels, and some lab and animal studies suggest vitamin C may help the body handle alcohol-related oxidative stress. On paper, it makes sense that more vitamin C might mean a milder hangover.

**The human evidence.** It's thin. Most studies on vitamins and hangovers are small, short, and often test multi-ingredient products, so it's hard to tell what any single vitamin is doing. Researchers who have surveyed drinkers about their diet (including work led by Joris Verster's group in the Netherlands, which looks at hangover severity) found some links between certain nutrients and milder hangovers, but this kind of study shows associations, not cause and effect. People who eat well may also drink differently, sleep better, and so on.

Systematic reviews of hangover remedies, such as a recent systematic review in the journal *Addiction* that looked across a long list of products and compounds, have consistently concluded that the evidence for any single hangover remedy is weak or very low quality. Vitamin C is no exception.

**What that means in practice:**

- If you eat a reasonably normal diet, you're probably not short on vitamin C, and one glass of juice fills the tank for the day anyway.
- Your body doesn't store extra vitamin C well. Above a certain amount, you absorb less and excrete the rest in urine. Taking huge doses doesn't create a bigger effect.
- There's no good evidence that vitamin C helps your liver clear alcohol or acetaldehyde faster in a way you'd feel.

So the vitamin C in orange juice won't hurt, but it's not the hero ingredient. For a wider look at which vitamins have any real support, see our guide to [vitamins for a hangover](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover).

## Does the Sugar in Orange Juice Help?

This is probably the most useful thing orange juice does for a hangover, though it comes with caveats.

**Why it can help.** Alcohol interferes with gluconeogenesis, the process your liver uses to make and release glucose when you haven't eaten. After a night of drinking, especially if you skipped dinner or danced for hours, your blood sugar can dip lower than usual. That can leave you shaky, weak, irritable, and foggy. A glass of juice is a fast, easy way to get some sugar back into your system when solid food sounds awful.

It's worth being honest that studies haven't found a strong, consistent link between blood sugar levels and overall hangover severity. Low blood sugar seems to explain some symptoms in some people, not the whole hangover. But if you feel shaky and drained and haven't eaten, juice is a reasonable first step.

**The fructose myth.** You may have heard that the fructose in fruit juice "burns off" alcohol faster. Some older lab research did suggest that fructose can modestly speed up how quickly the body clears alcohol, but the results were small and inconsistent. In practice, your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace (roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, though it varies). Orange juice won't sober you up, and it won't make you safe to drive.

**The caveats.**

- **It's a lot of sugar with no fiber.** A cup of juice has about as much sugar as several oranges, but without the fiber that slows its absorption. Pair it with food (eggs, toast, oatmeal) so you don't get a quick spike followed by a slump.
- **People with diabetes should be careful.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar for hours after drinking, and juice can raise it fast. If you have diabetes, check your levels rather than guessing, and follow your care plan.

## Orange Juice and Hydration: Better Than Water?

Not really. Orange juice is mostly water, so it does count toward rehydrating you. But for most hangovers, it's not a better rehydration tool than plain water, and for some situations it's worse than an electrolyte drink.

Here's why. When you've lost a lot of fluid, especially through sweating or vomiting, your body needs both water and **sodium** to hold on to that fluid. Oral rehydration solutions are designed with a specific balance of sodium and glucose for exactly this reason. Orange juice has plenty of potassium and sugar but almost no sodium. Very sugary drinks can also pull water into the gut and, for some people, worsen loose stools.

A practical way to think about it:

- **Mild hangover, no vomiting:** water plus a small glass of juice with breakfast is fine.
- **You sweated a lot (hot night, dancing):** add an electrolyte drink or something salty to eat.
- **You've been vomiting or have diarrhea:** start with small sips of an oral rehydration solution or electrolyte drink. Hold off on juice until your stomach settles.

If you want a deeper comparison, our guide to [electrolyte drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) breaks down the main options, and our look at [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) covers another potassium-rich alternative that's less acidic.

## The Acidity Problem: When Orange Juice Makes It Worse

This is the downside most hangover articles skip.

Alcohol increases stomach acid production and irritates the stomach lining. It also relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, the ring of muscle that keeps stomach acid from splashing up into your esophagus. That's why so many people wake up with heartburn, a sour taste, or a burning stomach after drinking.

Orange juice is acidic, with a pH typically around 3.3 to 4. Citrus is one of the most commonly reported heartburn triggers. Pouring a big glass of cold juice onto an already irritated stomach can make the burning worse, and for some people it brings on nausea.

**Signs juice probably isn't a good idea right now:**

- Heartburn or a burning feeling behind your breastbone
- A sore, burning, or "raw" stomach
- You've been vomiting
- You have known acid reflux, gastritis, or a stomach ulcer

**If you still want it:**

- Wait until you've had some water and a few bites of something bland, like toast or crackers.
- Dilute it half and half with water.
- Try a low-acid orange juice, which some brands sell for people with sensitive stomachs.
- Sip slowly rather than gulping.

If heartburn is a regular part of your mornings after drinking, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains the causes and what tends to help. For general stomach trouble, see our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## Orange Juice vs. Other Hangover Drinks

Here's an honest comparison of the drinks people most often reach for. None of these is a cure; they just do different jobs.

| Drink | Main strengths | Main weaknesses | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Water | Free, gentle, rehydrates | No electrolytes or energy | Every hangover, as the base |
| Orange juice | Sugar, potassium, vitamin C, tastes good | Acidic, little sodium, lots of sugar | Mild hangover with a calm stomach |
| Electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution | Sodium plus glucose, built for rehydration | Some are sugary or artificially flavored | After sweating, vomiting, or diarrhea |
| Coconut water | Potassium, lower acid, lighter taste | Lower sodium than rehydration drinks | Mild dehydration, sensitive stomach |
| Ginger tea | May ease nausea | Little fluid or energy beyond the tea itself | Queasiness |
| Coffee | Helps with grogginess | Can irritate the stomach, mild diuretic effect | After you've had water and food |

For more options ranked side by side, see our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

## Fresh, From Concentrate, or Whole Oranges?

**Fresh-squeezed vs. carton.** Nutritionally, they're close. Fresh juice may have slightly more vitamin C, and vitamin C slowly breaks down in an opened carton. Many commercial juices are pasteurized and some are fortified with calcium or vitamin D. For a hangover, any 100% orange juice is fine. Skip "orange drinks" or "juice cocktails," which are mostly added sugar and water.

**Pulp or no pulp.** Pulp adds a small amount of fiber. It won't make much difference to how you feel, so pick whichever you can stomach.

**Whole oranges.** If you can manage to eat one, a whole orange is in some ways better than juice. You still get vitamin C, potassium, and water, but the fiber slows the sugar hit and keeps you full. The downside is that chewing and digesting fruit can feel like too much when you're nauseated. Oranges are still acidic, so the same heartburn caution applies.

## Screwdrivers and Mimosas: Not a Hangover Cure

Plenty of brunch menus pair orange juice with alcohol, and the "hair of the dog" idea says a little more alcohol the next morning eases a hangover. It doesn't fix anything. It postpones the crash by putting more alcohol into your system, which your body then has to process all over again, and it adds to dehydration and sleep disruption. Over time, regularly drinking to feel better the morning after is a pattern worth noticing.

The orange juice in a mimosa or screwdriver doesn't cancel out the alcohol. If you want juice the morning after, drink it plain.

## Orange Juice and Medications

Most people can drink orange juice with common medicines, but there are a few things to know:

- **Some drugs absorb poorly with fruit juice.** The allergy medicine fexofenadine (Allegra) is meant to be taken with water, because fruit juices including orange juice can reduce how much of it your body absorbs.
- **Grapefruit is the bigger troublemaker.** Grapefruit juice interacts with a long list of prescription drugs. Orange juice causes far fewer of these problems, but blood orange and Seville (bitter) orange contain some of the same compounds as grapefruit. If you take regular prescription medicine, check with your pharmacist about juices in general.
- **Painkillers after drinking have their own risks.** Taking juice with a painkiller doesn't make the combination of painkiller and alcohol safer. If you're considering acetaminophen or ibuprofen the morning after, read the alcohol warnings on the label first.
- **Diabetes medication.** As noted above, alcohol can lower blood sugar, and juice raises it quickly. If you use insulin or medicines that lower blood sugar, monitor rather than guess.

When in doubt, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. They can look at your full medication list and give you an answer that fits your situation.

## A Smarter Hangover Morning (With or Without Orange Juice)

If you want a simple plan, here's one that uses orange juice where it helps and avoids it where it doesn't:

1. **Start with water.** A large glass when you wake up, then keep sipping through the morning. Pale yellow urine is a reasonable sign you're catching up.
2. **Check your stomach.** If it's calm, have a small glass of orange juice (around 4 to 8 ounces). If it's burning or queasy, choose an electrolyte drink or coconut water first.
3. **Eat something real.** Eggs, toast, oatmeal, or a banana give you steady energy and help buffer the juice's sugar and acid. Our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why eggs come up so often.
4. **Add electrolytes if you sweated or vomited.** Sodium matters more than vitamin C here.
5. **Rest.** Time is still the only thing that reliably ends a hangover. Sleep if you can.
6. **Be careful with painkillers.** Read the label, take the lowest dose that works, and don't take acetaminophen if you drink heavily on a regular basis without asking a doctor first.

## Prevention Beats Any Morning Drink

No glass of juice can undo a heavy night. The things that most reliably reduce hangovers happen before and during drinking: eating a proper meal first, pacing yourself, alternating alcoholic drinks with water, and simply drinking less. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best support, and our piece on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why food matters so much.

Some people also add a supplement to their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven, and it doesn't replace eating, hydrating, or drinking less. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine, check with your doctor before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Orange juice can help a mild hangover a little by giving you fluid, quick sugar, and potassium when food feels hard.
- The vitamin C is the least proven part. There is no good evidence that it shortens a hangover, and one glass already covers your daily needs.
- It's acidic. If you have heartburn, a burning stomach, or you've been vomiting, start with water or an electrolyte drink and a bland snack instead.
- It's low in sodium, so it isn't the best choice for serious rehydration after sweating or vomiting.
- Don't mix it with more alcohol, and don't rely on it to sober you up.
- Get medical help for signs of alcohol poisoning, vomiting you can't stop, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, or confusion.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is orange juice good for a hangover?**

It can help a little, mostly because it gets fluid, sugar, and potassium into you when you don't feel like eating. It is not a cure. There is no good evidence that orange juice, or the vitamin C in it, shortens a hangover in a meaningful way. Its acidity can also make heartburn or an upset stomach worse, so if your stomach is rough, start with water and something bland and save the juice for later.

**Does vitamin C help a hangover?**

Probably not by much. Heavy drinking can lower vitamin C levels, and vitamin C is an antioxidant, so the idea makes sense on paper. But the human studies on vitamin C and hangovers are small and mixed, and none show it reliably fixes how you feel. If you eat a normal diet, a glass of orange juice already covers more than a day's worth of vitamin C, so extra pills are unlikely to add much.

**Is orange juice bad for an upset stomach after drinking?**

It can be. Orange juice is acidic, and alcohol already irritates the stomach lining and loosens the valve that keeps stomach acid out of your esophagus. If you have heartburn, a burning stomach, or you've been vomiting, juice may sting. Wait until your stomach settles, dilute it with water, and have it with food. If you have frequent reflux, a low-acid drink like water, coconut water, or an electrolyte drink is gentler.

**Is orange juice better than Gatorade for a hangover?**

They do different jobs. Orange juice has more vitamin C and potassium and no added coloring, but almost no sodium. Sports drinks have sodium, which helps your body hold on to fluid, but little else. If you've been sweating or vomiting, an electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution is the better rehydration tool. If you just want fluid and some easy calories, juice is fine. Many people do best with water plus a small glass of juice.

**Does orange juice speed up alcohol metabolism?**

Not in any way you'd notice. Some older lab research suggested fructose, a sugar found in fruit juice, might slightly speed up how fast the body clears alcohol, but the effect was small and inconsistent, and it does not make you sober faster. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many people. Juice won't change that enough to matter for driving or anything else.

**Is a screwdriver or mimosa a good hangover cure?**

No. Adding vodka or champagne to orange juice is a version of hair of the dog, which only delays the hangover by adding more alcohol. The juice doesn't cancel out the drink. If you want orange juice the morning after, drink it plain.

**Can I drink orange juice with medication after drinking?**

Usually, but check the label. Orange juice can lower the absorption of a few drugs, including the allergy medicine fexofenadine (Allegra), which is meant to be taken with water. Grapefruit juice causes far more drug interactions than orange juice, but if you take regular prescription medicine, ask your pharmacist whether any juice is a problem. If you're on diabetes medication, also be careful: alcohol can push blood sugar down and juice can push it up quickly.
